title: Feelings with a Sliding Scale
objectives: I can name strong and gentle feelings with ten new words.
I can put feeling words in order from a little to a lot.
I can use a character's actions to figure out how the character feels.
I can write about a time I felt a strong feeling.
rationale: Third graders know happy, mad, sad, and scared. This unit gives them graded feeling words so they can say how strongly a character feels and why. The ten words sit on sliding scales: anger (furious), fear (anxious, terrified), joy (delighted), confusion (puzzled, bewildered), surprise (astonished), and pressure or low mood (overwhelmed, exhausted, miserable). Students practice proving a feeling word with an action or a detail in the text, which prepares them for character analysis in later grades.

words.def: Very happy and pleased about something.
words.ex: Maya was delighted when her grandmother arrived with a surprise gift.
words.ex2: The delighted puppy spun in circles at the sight of its leash.
words.nonExample: A child who frowns and sighs at a party is not delighted.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: The author tells us the hero is delighted by showing her big smile.
apps.spoken: I am delighted that you came to my game.
apps.writing: Use delighted when a character is more than just happy.

cloze.s: Ben was ___ when his team won, and he jumped up and cheered.

cloze2.s: The audience was ___ by the funny puppet show and laughed all the way through it.

misuse.s: She was delighted when her ice cream fell on the sidewalk, and she began to cry.
misuse.why: Delighted means very happy; crying over fallen ice cream does not fit.

visual.alt: A smiling child opening a gift.

words.def: So very angry that you may want to shout.
words.ex: Dad was furious when the dog chewed up his new shoes.
words.ex2: The furious crowd booed when the game was called off.
words.nonExample: Feeling a little bit bothered by a loud noise is not being furious.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: The character's clenched fists show that she is furious, not just annoyed.
apps.spoken: I was furious when someone broke my model.
apps.writing: Use furious for the top of the anger scale.

cloze.s: Tia was ___ when her brother broke her model, and her face turned bright red.

cloze2.s: The ___ cat hissed and puffed up its fur when the dog stole its food.

misuse.s: He was furious about the surprise party and thanked everyone with a gentle smile.
misuse.why: Furious means extremely angry; a gentle smile and thank-you do not show that.

visual.alt: An angry face with anger marks beside it.

words.def: Worried and nervous about what might happen.
words.ex: Jo felt anxious on the first day at her new school.
words.ex2: The anxious dog paced by the door until its owner came home.
words.nonExample: Someone who is calm and ready for a test is not anxious.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: A character can feel anxious before a big event, such as a test.
apps.spoken: I get anxious when I have to speak in front of the class.
apps.writing: Use anxious when a character worries about the future.

cloze.s: The ___ boy kept checking the clock, worried that the bus would be late for the field trip.

cloze2.s: Mia was ___ before the spelling bee, and her hands shook as she waited for her turn.

misuse.s: He felt anxious because he knew nothing could possibly go wrong, so he napped happily.
misuse.why: Anxious means worried about what might happen; a happy nap shows no worry.

visual.alt: A worried face next to a clock.

words.def: Unable to understand something and trying to figure it out.
words.ex: Leo looked puzzled when the magic trick ended with an empty box.
words.ex2: The teacher gave a puzzled frown at the strange note on her desk.
words.nonExample: A student who knows the answer right away is not puzzled.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: A puzzled reader goes back and rereads to find the answer.
apps.spoken: I was puzzled by the directions, so I asked a friend.
apps.writing: Use puzzled when a character cannot make sense of something yet.

cloze.s: The ___ girl scratched her head, because the door was open and she was sure she had locked it.

cloze2.s: Sam was ___ when the map showed a river where he saw only a field.

misuse.s: She was puzzled because she understood every step and finished with ease.
misuse.why: Puzzled means not understanding; finishing with ease shows she understood.

visual.alt: A thinking face next to a question mark.

words.def: Very surprised, as if you can hardly believe it.
words.ex: The children were astonished when the magician pulled a rabbit from his hat.
words.ex2: I was astonished to find my lost watch in the garden.
words.nonExample: Seeing the same old tree on your street every day is not astonishing.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: Authors show an astonished character with wide eyes and an open mouth.
apps.spoken: I was astonished by how tall the tower was.
apps.writing: Use astonished for a surprise that is bigger than just surprised.

cloze.s: Rosa was ___ when she opened the box and found a real kitten inside.

cloze2.s: The explorers were ___ by the huge cave, with walls that sparkled like stars.

misuse.s: He was astonished by the sunrise because it came up at the same time as always, and he barely looked up.
misuse.why: Astonished means greatly surprised; a normal sunrise that he barely notices does not fit.

visual.alt: A surprised face next to a magician's hat.

words.def: So tired that you have no energy left.
words.ex: After the long hike, the exhausted campers fell asleep right away.
words.ex2: Dad was exhausted from carrying boxes up three flights of stairs.
words.nonExample: A person who feels full of energy after a nap is not exhausted.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: Explorers in a story may feel exhausted after a long journey.
apps.spoken: I was exhausted after the race, so I sat down.
apps.writing: Use exhausted for being much more tired than sleepy.

cloze.s: The ___ runner crossed the finish line and dropped to the grass, too tired to speak.

cloze2.s: After playing outside all day in the heat, Kai was ___ and went to bed early.

misuse.s: The exhausted swimmer jumped out of the pool, full of energy, and ran three more laps.
misuse.why: Exhausted means no energy left, but running three more laps shows plenty of energy.

visual.alt: A tired face next to a bed.

words.def: Feeling like there is too much to handle at one time.
words.ex: Zoe felt overwhelmed by the huge pile of homework on her desk.
words.ex2: The new puppy was overwhelmed by all the loud children at the party.
words.nonExample: Doing one small job with a calm mind does not leave you overwhelmed.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: A character may feel overwhelmed when many problems come at once.
apps.spoken: I felt overwhelmed by so many choices, so I made a list.
apps.writing: Use overwhelmed when there is too much going on for a character to manage.

cloze.s: The ___ cook did not know which pot to stir first, because six orders came in at once.

cloze2.s: Dee felt ___ on her first day at the huge, noisy fair, with so many people and rides around her.

misuse.s: She felt overwhelmed because she had only one small task and plenty of time.
misuse.why: Overwhelmed means too much at once; one small task with plenty of time is easy.

visual.alt: A dizzy face beside a tall stack of books.

words.def: So confused that you feel lost and cannot think clearly.
words.ex: The bewildered tourist turned the map around and around.
words.ex2: Ava stood bewildered in the crowded hall, unsure which way to go.
words.nonExample: A student who follows the directions easily is not bewildered.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: In a story, a bewildered character often asks, "What is going on?"
apps.spoken: I felt bewildered when all the signs changed.
apps.writing: Use bewildered for confusion that is stronger than puzzled.

cloze.s: The ___ new student wandered the halls, unable to find any room on her schedule.

cloze2.s: Everyone spoke at once, and the ___ visitor did not know whom to answer first.

misuse.s: He stood bewildered because he knew exactly where to go and walked straight there.
misuse.why: Bewildered means very confused; knowing exactly where to go is the opposite.

visual.alt: A dizzy face beside a compass.

words.def: So scared that you may freeze or run.
words.ex: The terrified kitten hid under the bed during the thunderstorm.
words.ex2: Luis was terrified when he heard footsteps behind him in the dark.
words.nonExample: A person who feels only a bit nervous is not terrified.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: Authors show a terrified character with a pounding heart and shaking hands.
apps.spoken: I was terrified of the big slide until I tried it.
apps.writing: Use terrified for the top of the fear scale.

cloze.s: The ___ hikers froze when a bear stepped onto the path just a few feet away.

cloze2.s: Her heart pounded and her knees shook, because she was ___ of the dark cave.

misuse.s: He was terrified of the puppy, so he laughed and gave it a big hug.
misuse.why: Terrified means extremely scared; laughing and hugging shows no fear.

visual.alt: A scared face under a stormy sky.

words.ex: The cold, wet campers felt miserable as the rain poured down.
words.ex2: Sofia was miserable on the bus ride, because she missed her friends.
words.nonExample: Feeling cozy and warm by the fire is not being miserable.
words.rel: feelings from a little to a lot

apps.academic: The author shows a miserable day with cold rain and a sad face.
apps.spoken: I felt miserable with a fever and a sore throat.
apps.writing: Use miserable when a character is both very sad and uncomfortable.

cloze.s: The ___ puppy sat in the rain with drooping ears, cold and soaked to the skin.

cloze2.s: Lily felt ___ when she had the flu, with a fever, a sore throat, and nobody to play with.

misuse.s: The miserable boy sang and danced all afternoon because he was so happy.
misuse.why: Miserable means very unhappy; singing and dancing show happiness.

visual.alt: A sad face under a rain cloud.

words.frame: A miserable day is one when ___.

passage.title: Nora at the Fair
paras: Nora was delighted when her mom said they could go to the fair. She had saved her coins for weeks. At the gate, she felt anxious, because she could not find her ticket anywhere.

"Where could it be?" she asked, puzzled. She emptied her pockets twice. Her little brother, Ty, giggled. Then Nora saw the ticket sticking out of his shoe. "You took it!" she exclaimed. She was furious, but Mom gave Ty a stern look, and he said sorry.

Inside, the fair was loud and bright. There were so many rides, games, and smells that Nora felt overwhelmed. She turned in a circle, bewildered, not sure where to go first. Then a clown pulled a rabbit from an empty hat, and she was astonished.

The tallest ride made her terrified, so she chose the carousel instead. When she dropped her ice cream, she felt miserable for a minute, until Ty shared his. By evening, Nora was exhausted. She leaned on Mom's shoulder and smiled all the way home.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "overwhelmed" most nearly means
choices: feeling there was too much at once
qs.why: Nora sees many rides, games, and smells at once and does not know where to start, so there is too much for her to handle.

qs.q: Why did Mom give Ty a stern look?
choices: She wanted him to buy more tickets.
She thought he had taken Nora's ticket and it was not kind.
She wanted him to ride the carousel.
qs.why: Ty had hidden Nora's ticket in his shoe, so Mom looked at him sternly.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Nora was astonished?
choices: She saved her coins for weeks.
A clown pulled a rabbit from an empty hat.
qs.why: The surprising trick is what made her astonished.

qs.q: What is a central idea of the story?
choices: Brothers should never go to fairs.
Nora has many different feelings in one day.
qs.why: The story moves from delighted to anxious, furious, overwhelmed, astonished, terrified, miserable, and exhausted.

write.prompt: Write about a day when you had more than one feeling. Use at least three words from this unit.
write.frame: At first I felt ___, but then I felt ___ because ___.

study.task: Choose two feeling words that go on the same scale, such as puzzled and bewildered. Draw a line, put the words in order from weaker to stronger, and write one sentence for each.

groups.label: strong feelings of anger and fear
feelings of joy, stress, and tiredness

sentences: Write a sentence about a time you felt anxious. Tell what you did to feel better.
Write a sentence that uses both puzzled and clue.
Write a sentence about what makes a person feel exhausted. Use because.
Write a sentence about something that would leave you astonished.

given: She did not know where to start.
She felt too much at once.
combine.model: Rosa felt overwhelmed because she had so many chores that she did not know where to start.

discuss: What is the difference between puzzled and bewildered? Give an example of each.
What can you do when you feel anxious?
Which feeling word is stronger: upset or furious? How do you know?
produce.explain: Explain how an author can show that a character is terrified without using the word. Give two details.

argue.prompt: Claim: It is helpful to use exact feeling words instead of just happy, sad, mad, or scared. Do you agree? Give two reasons.
argue.frame: I think exact words help because ___. For example, ___ is stronger than ___.

constructed.prompt: Write about two characters on the same rainy day. One is delighted and one is miserable. Tell why.
look: gives a reason for each feeling
constructed.model: Ben was delighted because he loved jumping in puddles. His sister was miserable because her shoes were soaked and she wanted to stay dry.

constructed.prompt: Put puzzled and bewildered in order from weaker to stronger. Use each in a sentence that shows the difference.
look: puts them in a sensible order
constructed.model: Mia was puzzled by the riddle, but she was bewildered when all the lights went out and she lost her way. Bewildered is a stronger kind of confusion.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten graded feeling words, read a story that moves through many feelings in one day, and practice placing feeling words on sliding scales before using them in writing.

notes.va.delighted.adj: Delighted is stronger than happy. Ask students to show the difference with a face and a voice.
notes.va.furious.adj: Furious is the top of the anger ladder. Use the ladder annoyed, upset, angry, furious and have students place real events on it.
notes.va.anxious.adj: Anxious is worry about what might happen. Link to uneasy from the earlier unit. It is a normal feeling, so talk about calm-down tools.
notes.va.puzzled.adj: Puzzled is mild confusion that can be solved with thinking. Contrast with bewildered, which is much stronger.
notes.va.astonished.adj: Astonished is greater than surprised. Act out a small surprise and a huge one so students feel the difference.
notes.va.exhausted.adj: Exhausted is more than tired. Ask students what makes their body feel exhausted versus sleepy.
notes.va.overwhelmed.adj: Overwhelmed is about too much at once, not only sadness. Ask what could help: one thing at a time.
notes.va.bewildered.adj: Bewildered is deep confusion; the person feels lost. Use the picture of a lost compass.
notes.va.terrified.adj: Terrified is the top of the fear ladder. Read a sentence with a terrified character and have students find clues like shaking hands.
notes.va.miserable.adj: Miserable includes being uncomfortable, such as cold or sick, as well as very unhappy.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: "Nora cannot find her ticket and checks the clock. She is worried about what will happen, so anxious fits. When she sees the ticket in Ty's shoe, her feeling is stronger than annoyed, so I would choose furious. I can prove each word with a detail."
discuss: Which feeling in the story would be hardest to handle? Why?
How does Nora's mood change from the start to the end of the day?
misconceptions: Puzzled and bewildered mean the same thing.
Anxious means scared of something right in front of you.
extend: Make a feelings thermometer for anger or fear with five words in order.
Rewrite a short story scene using stronger feeling words in place of mad and sad.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the anger and fear ladders two days later and again at one week; use gloomy, uneasy, and exclaim when writing about a character's mood in the next story.

wida.oral: Partner A makes a face or body pose for a feeling word without speaking; Partner B names the word and says one clue that helped.
